## [Executive Summary](#_sbfa50wo7nsh)
The Gaming Room is expanding their mobile application, Draw It or Lose It, from an Android-only format into a multi-platform, web-based application. The main challenge faced is refactoring the existing single-platform codebase to support concurrent instances of multiplayer games. Additionally, we must enforce unique naming constraints and maintain memory efficiency across all distributed platforms.

To resolve these challenges, we propose refactoring the existing codebase. We propose doing this by implementing the singleton design pattern to provide system wide management. We also propose implementing the iterator design pattern to create a system for data retrieval. Together, these design patterns will reliably enforce business rules, eliminate data redundancy, and ensure high scalability. 

## Requirements
- Business requirements

  - Transition the Android based game to web-based, multiplatform game

  - Support multiple teams per game session and multiple players per team

  - Enforce unique names for games and teams during game creation 

- Technical requirements

  - Maintain only one instance of the game management engine in memory at any given time

  - Prevent duplicate entities of teams or players by iterating through existing collections of entities

  - Abstract common properties across entities through an extensible class hierarchy
## [Design Constraints](#_2et92p0)
**Single Game Instantiation:** In a distributed web environment, multiple client connections interact simultaneously. Ensuring only one instance of the game management engine exists prevents inconsistent memory states across concurrent user requests. 

**Network and Memory Overhead:** Web applications must minimize the server's memory payload size. With multiple clients making requests to the same server, iterating through game entities in memory but being optimized so that checking name uniqueness does not bottleneck performance during peak traffic.

**Platform Independence:** Since this new version of the game will be web-based and cross platform, data structures must remain decoupled from platform-specific frameworks such as an Android specific API. This will require standard Java object architecture to run cleanly on a web server host.

## [Domain Model](#_8h2ehzxfam4o)
- **Class relationship and structure**

  - **Entity (base class):** This is an abstract class that holds common attributes and their associated getters and setters.

  - **Derived classes (Game, Team, Player):** Each of these classes inherits directly from the Entity base class. A Game contains one or more Team instances and each Team contains multiple Player instances. 

- **OOP principles applied**

  - **Inheritance**: Extends the Entity class into Game, Team, and Player, reducing redundant code by centralizing the identifier and name attributes in the superclass.

  - **Encapsulation**: Keeps data fields private within the Entity class and exposes them safely with public methods, protecting internal state integrity.

  - **Abstraction**: Hides general entity attributes behind the Entity contract as private variables, allowing the GameService class to interact with high-level abstractions rather than duplicate code across separate models

## Recommendations
Analyze the characteristics of and techniques specific to various systems architectures and make a recommendation to The Gaming Room. Specifically, address the following:

**Operating Platform**: We recommend a cloud-hosted Linux operating platform to host this web application. We recommend Linux because it is a lightweight and cost-effective hosting environment for Java back-end services. We recommend a web-based client because it moves away from platform-specific native clients, allowing for seamless functionality across all user platforms.

**Operating Systems Architectures**: The back end consists of Java-based RESTful web services deployed inside lightweight Linux containers. A reverse proxy handles SSL termination, load balancing, and routing HTTP requests to the appropriate Java service instances. The client-side architecture utilizes a SPA framework rendered in the user’s browser. This will decouple the client UI from back-end business logic.

**Storage Management**: To support real-time multiplayer gameplay alongside persistent player data, we recommend implementing a hybrid storage architecture on the Linux host. A managed relational database system will securely store structured persistent data including user profiles, account credentials, and match histories. For low-latency multiplayer operations, an in-memory database like Redis will manage live session states. Additionally, static game assets such as images, UI graphics, and client-side code bundles are offloaded to cloud object storage. This approach balances strong data integrity with quick retrieval speeds during active gameplay.

**Memory Management**: The recommended platform manages memory allocation dynamically across both server runtime and client browser environments. On the server side, the Linux-hosted Java application will use built-in Garbage Collection algorithms to automatically free memory from finished game sessions. Linux container limits are strictly configured to allocate predictable memory boundaries and prevent system-level out-of-memory crashes. On the client side, modern web browsers utilize automatic JavaScript garbage collection to free unreferenced objects during active play. To optimize performance on memory-constrained mobile devices, client scripts are designed to clean up unmounted components and disconnect idle WebSocket listeners.

**Distributed Systems and Networks**: To facilitate seamless communication across user devices, the game leverages standard network protocols over a distributed architecture. Stateless operations, such as account authentication and retrieving player records, communicate via secure HTTPS REST APIs. Real-time gameplay features utilize persistent web socket connections to maintain low-latency communication. A cloud load balancer distributes incoming network connections across redundant Linux application nodes to ensure high availability. In the event of temporary network disruptions or mobile handoffs, session tokens allow clients to reconnect and sync back into active game states without losing progress.

**Security**: End-to-end security measures protect user data both in transit across networks and at rest within the operating environment. All communication between client web browsers and the Linux server is encrypted using TLS 1.3 for HTTPS and secure web sockets to prevent monitoring. On the server side, input sanitization and strict validation are enforced on all drawing coordinates and chat messages to mitigate cross-site scripting and SQL Injection vulnerabilities. Finally, the Linux server infrastructure is hardened using automated OS security patches and strict firewall rules.
